flashcards.front: Low-skilled vs high-skilled adversary: how do you tell them apart?
flashcards.back_definition: Low-skilled attackers run existing public tools they do not fully understand. High-skilled attackers write or modify their own tools, understand the protocols, and may use undisclosed (zero-day) flaws.
flashcards.back_example: Running a downloaded packet sniffer at a cafe vs writing a custom exploit for a router bug nobody has reported.
flashcards.back_confusion: Low skill does not mean low risk: free tools make attacks cheap, so there are many more of them.

flashcards.back_definition: A flaw the vendor does not know about yet, so no patch exists and defenders have had zero days of warning.
flashcards.back_example: A spyware vendor sells a zero-day phone exploit that has been used against journalists.
flashcards.back_confusion: Once a patch is released the flaw is no longer a zero-day, even though unpatched systems stay exposed.

flashcards.front: How does an attacker's motivation shape the attack?
flashcards.back_definition: Money drives broad, opportunistic sweeps; espionage and sabotage drive patient, targeted attacks on specific people; curiosity or disruption drive noisy ones.
flashcards.back_example: DarkHotel targeted chosen executives on hotel Wi-Fi rather than every guest.
flashcards.back_confusion: Feeling you have nothing worth stealing does not protect you: opportunists resell any credential in bulk.
flashcards.back_hook: Why they attack tells you who they pick.

flashcards.back_definition: A rogue access point that broadcasts the same network name (SSID) as a trusted network, so victims connect to it and their traffic passes through the attacker.
flashcards.back_example: Two "AirportFree" networks appear: one WPA2, one open with a stronger signal.
flashcards.back_confusion: A rogue AP is any unauthorised access point; an evil twin specifically imitates a legitimate network's name.

flashcards.back_definition: The SSID is the human-readable network name. The BSSID is the MAC address of the radio broadcasting it, unique to each access point.
flashcards.back_confusion: Several BSSIDs for one SSID is normal in a big office; an unknown BSSID for a small cafe network is suspicious.
flashcards.back_hook: SSID is the name tag; BSSID is the fingerprint.

flashcards.front: What does an evil twin let the attacker do once you join?
flashcards.back_definition: Act as a man-in-the-middle: read or change unencrypted traffic, show a fake captive portal to harvest logins, and try SSL stripping.
flashcards.back_example: A fake portal asks for social media credentials before "granting internet access".
flashcards.back_confusion: HTTPS with a valid certificate still protects the content; the danger is plain HTTP, fake portals and ignored certificate warnings.

flashcards.front: What is SSL stripping, and what defeats it?
flashcards.back_definition: A man-in-the-middle keeps HTTPS with the server but serves the victim plain HTTP, so the victim's traffic is readable. HSTS (RFC 6797) makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for that site.
flashcards.back_example: The address bar shows http://bank.example with no padlock where you expected https.
flashcards.back_confusion: SSL stripping does not break encryption; it stops it from being used at all.
flashcards.back_hook: No padlock where there should be one = stop.

flashcards.front: How does RF jamming deny Wi-Fi service?
flashcards.back_definition: The jammer floods the channel with radio noise. Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA, so devices sense the noise and keep backing off, and nothing gets sent.
flashcards.back_example: The noise floor on channel 6 stays near -40 dBm for many consecutive samples.
flashcards.back_confusion: A microwave oven causes brief interference; jamming is sustained over many consecutive measurements.
flashcards.back_hook: Shouting so no one else can talk.

flashcards.back_definition: Received Signal Strength Indicator: the power of a received radio signal, measured in dBm and, for Wi-Fi, always a negative number. Closer to zero is stronger.
flashcards.back_example: -45 dBm is a strong signal; -85 dBm is weak.
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't read -40 as weaker than -80: -40 is the stronger signal.

flashcards.back_definition: Moving through an area with a wireless scanner to log networks: SSIDs, BSSIDs, security types, signal strength and GPS location.
flashcards.back_example: An attacker finds a company's SSID in a public war-driving map and names it in a phishing email.
flashcards.back_confusion: War driving is reconnaissance; it maps targets but does not by itself break into anything.

flashcards.front: Why is an open Wi-Fi network risky?
flashcards.back_definition: With no password, the radio link is unencrypted, so anyone nearby can capture the traffic, and anyone can set up a network with the same name.
flashcards.back_example: Plain HTTP form logins on cafe Wi-Fi can be read by a laptop at the next table.
flashcards.back_confusion: A shared password (WPA2-PSK) does not stop the network operator, or a fake access point, from seeing your traffic.

flashcards.front: What does a VPN protect on public Wi-Fi, and what does it not?
flashcards.back_definition: It encrypts traffic from your device to the VPN server, so the local network sees only an encrypted tunnel. It does not hide anything from the VPN provider, and it does not protect you from phishing pages or malware.
flashcards.back_example: Turning the VPN off to log into a captive portal leaves that window unprotected.
flashcards.back_confusion: A VPN moves trust from the cafe to the VPN provider; it does not remove the need for trust.
flashcards.back_hook: A tunnel protects the road, not the destination.

flashcards.front: Put the safe public Wi-Fi steps in order.
flashcards.back_definition: 1 Confirm the exact network name with staff. 2 Avoid open networks for sensitive work. 3 Turn on a VPN before browsing. 4 Use HTTPS only and heed certificate warnings. 5 Turn off auto-join.
flashcards.back_example: Ask the librarian for the exact SSID before you join.
flashcards.back_confusion: SSID verification comes first: a VPN started after joining an evil twin may already be too late.
